                    Introduction


K
       erala has long relied on agriculture and its allied sectors not only as a key
       source of livelihood but also as a fundamental driver of its cultural and
       economic evolution. The state's agricultural history is deeply intertwined
with trade and commerce, particularly due to its unique spice cultivation. Spices
such as pepper, clove, cardamom, ginger, and turmeric, grown along the fertile
valleys of the Western Ghats, have attracted traders from across the world for
centuries, leading interregional and international trade relationships. These
interactions played a significant role in shaping Kerala’s economic structure and
led to the introduction of several foreign crops that have since become integral to
the state's agricultural landscape. Notably, crops like rubber, papaya and
tapioca, which are now cultivated extensively, were not originally indigenous to
Kerala. Over time, these crops have seamlessly integrated into the state's
agrarian economy, with rubber, in particular, emerging as a major contributor to
Kerala’s overall agricultural output. This openness to adopting new crops and
agricultural practices remains a defining characteristic of the state’s agrarian
sector.
       Despite the historical significance of agriculture, recent trends highlight
concerns regarding its sustainability and economic contribution. While
agriculture continues to be vital for food security and rural livelihoods, its share
in Kerala's Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) has seen a significant decline
over the past decade. In 2011-12, the crop sector contributed 8.64% to the state’s
GSDP, but this figure has fallen to just 4.49% in 2023-24, according to the latest
real (constant price) estimates. This decline does not imply that the sector has
stopped growing; rather, it suggests that its growth has not kept pace with the
expansion of the secondary and tertiary sectors. The major contributors of
sector's Gross Value Output(GVO) are Rubber (20%), Coconut (19 %), Arecanut
(9%), Tapioca (7%) and Cardamom (7%). The detailed analysis of area,
production and productivity of crops of the state are given in the following
sections to portrait clear picture of crops sector of the state.

                         CHAPTER 1
                                        LAND USE
                                    STATISTICS 2023-24
                                 Land is a significant natural resource and is
                          required as an input in any production activity. Land use
                          statistics give information on identification of different
                          purposes of land according to their role and importance.
                          Land use transition and its dynamic changes are highly
                          affected by several socio-economic factors and
                          environmental factors. Major factors that influence land
                          use are topography, climate, soil type, population density,
                          technological changes, culture and traditions. From the
                          point of view of agriculture, land available for cultivation
                          is the most important among different land use patterns.

                                 Kerala has a diverse land use pattern with distinct
                          topography having agriculture as a dominant land use
                          type. The mixed cropping pattern, scale of farming and
                          very low per capita land holding is unique to Kerala. The
                          information on Land Use Pattern in Kerala is collected
                          through Land utilization Survey under EARAS scheme
                          in every agricultural year on the basis of 13 broad
                          classification of land use.

1. Forest


         Forest represents all actually forested area as the lands classed or
administered as forest under any legal enactment dealing with forest. The forest
area of the State during 2023- 24 was 10,81,509 Ha which is 27.83% of the total
geographical area of the State. Idukki district has the largest forest cover of
1,98,413 Ha (18.35%) in the State.

2. Land put to Non-Agricultural use


         The land put to use for purposes other than agriculture such as building,
pathways, roads, canals, rivers, bus stands, railways, local reservoirs, swamps etc.
are brought under this category. The area classified under this category amounts to
502608.91 Ha, representing 12.93% of the State's geographical area. Malappuram
district holds the highest record in this classification, with 61332.32 Ha (12.20%)
devoted to non-agricultural uses, followed closely by Palakkad district, which
accounts for 52455.74 Ha (10.44%).

 3. Barren and uncultivable land

         Land which cannot be brought under cultivation unless at a high cost,
whether such a land is in isolated blocks or within cultivated holdings, such as
mountains, deserts, hills etc are classified as barren and uncultivable land.
         The total land comes under this category is 9491.1 Ha which represents
0.24% of the total geographical area of the State. Kasaragode district has 2479.75
Ha which is 26.13 % of the state’s barren and uncultivable land.

 4. Permanent pastures and other grazing land

         Permanent pastures and other grazing lands cover all grazing lands,
whether they are permanent pastures or meadows or not. No area falls under this
category in 2023- 24.




     3    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                               Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




 5. Land under miscellaneous tree crops

         All cultivable lands, which is not included under net area sown, but is put to
some agricultural use such as land under casuarina trees, thatching grass, bamboo
bushes and other groves for fuel etc. comes under this category. Out of the total
geographical area, land under miscellaneous tree crops and groves are not included
in the net area sown and it occupies only 2050.46 Ha (0.05%).


   6. Cultivable waste


         These include land available for cultivation but not taken up for cultivation
or abandoned after a few years for one reason or the other. Such lands may be
either fallow or covered with shrubs and jungles, which are not put to any use. They
may be assessed or unassessed and may lie in isolated blocks or within cultivate
holdings. Lands once cultivated but remaining uncultivated for five years or more
in succession shall also be included in this category. The total area under cultivable
waste during 2023-24 is 102302.86 Ha ie.2.63% of the total geographical area of the
state. The area under this category is highest in Palakkad district accounting
21916.19 Ha (21.42%) and lowest in Thiruvananthapuram district accounting
920.86 Ha (0.9%).


   7. Fallow other than current fallow


         Land which were taken up for cultivation but have been temporarily put of
cultivation for a period of not less than one year but not more than five years due to
abject poverty of the cultivators, inadequate supply of water, silting of canals and
rivers etc are treated as other fallow land. The total area under other fallow land
during 2023-24 accounts 51227.44 Ha which is 1.32% of the total geographical area.
The land under this category is highest in Palakkad district with 12661.45 Ha
(24.72%) and lowest in Thiruvananthapuram district with 1027.71 Ha (2.01%).




     4    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                               Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala


   8. Current fallow
         This class comprises cropped areas, which are kept fallow during the
current year. The area under this category during 2023-24 is 57360.78 Ha, which
is 1.48% of total geographical area.

   9. Marshy land
         Land which gets permanently or periodically inundated by water and
characterized by vegetation which includes grasses and weeds. Out of the total
geographical area only 11.14 Ha come under marshy land during the year
2023-24.

  10. Still water
         The land under still water is broadly the land occupied by water bodies like
rivers, lakes, ponds, reservoirs, backwater, canals, tanks including nature made
deepsin which water stands still for most part of the period. This is the land on
which there is no vegetative growth of any kind. Out of the total geographical area,
101412.74 Ha of land is under still water constituting 2.61%. The land under still
water is highest in Palakkad district and the area is 15512.16 Ha. ie. 15.3% of the
total still water area.

  11. Water logged area
         It is the land where water is at / near the surface and stands for most part
of the year. It is generally found in low - lying areas and it excludes lakes, ponds
and tanks. The total water logged area for the year 2023-24 is 2936.72 Ha. It is
0.08% of the total geographical area of the state.

  12. Social Forestry

         The land under social forestry is the land in which the trees are planted by
the side of railway lines, road side, river and canal banks with a view to meet the
fuel and the fodder needs of the rural population and to serve the broader goals of
soil conservation and provision of shed and shelter for crops. It also includes village
forests/plantation which is being used by common man. An extent of 2606.13 Ha of
land comes under social forestry which is 0.07% of the total geographical area of
the state. The land under social forestry is highest in Idukki district and it is 1251
Ha (48%) followed by Palakkad district 352.45 Ha (13.52 %).


     5    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                             Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala


  13. Net Area Sown

     In calculating the net area sown, area sown more than once will be counted

only once. Area cultivated during any part of the agricultural year should come

under net area sown. Out of 38,86,287 Ha of total geographical area 1972769.72

Ha of land constituting 50.76% is cultivated once with various crops during the

year 2023-24. Idukki has the maximum net area sown (203039.25 Ha). Other

districts with significant net area sown include Palakkad (193857.67 Ha) and

Malappuram (168515.2 Ha). Pathanamthitta has the minimum net area sown

(77898.52 Ha). (see Fig.1)

Total Cropped Area (Gross Area Sown)

      The gross area sown represents the total area cultivated under all food and
non-food crops including the area sown more than once during the year 2023-24.
According to this concept the area under various crops in the same plot can be
more than the actual area. The gross area sown during 2023-24 was 2536423.217
Ha against 2515923.37 Ha in 2022- 23. The gross area sown is slightly increased
by 0.81% over the previous year. The percentage of cropped area to geographical
area in the districts of Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Malappuram
and Kozhikkod has increased from 2022-23 to 2023-24. In contrast, the
percentage of cropped area to geographical area in Palakkad district has
decreased over the same period. The percentages for other districts remain
unchanged.

                                         CHAPTER 2

                                   CROP AREA
                                STATISTICS 2023-24
                            The crop area statistics plays a vital role in
                    estimating crop production statistics. It helps to gather
                    information on the cropping pattern of an area and the
                    cropping intensity and its reflection in the agricultural
                    economy. The accuracy of crop production estimates is
                    depending on the accuracy of crop area statistics.

                            The cropping pattern of Kerala is entirely different
                    from other states due to its topography and the tropical
                    climate condition which suitable for growing various seasonal
                    crops such as paddy, vegetables and annual crops such as
                    tapioca, banana and many perennial crops such as plantation
                    crops and spices. The information on cropping pattern in
                    Kerala is collected through canvassing a bifurcated data of
                    Net Area Sown along with Land utilization Survey in each
                    season in every agricultural year.

                                          Cropped Area of Food Grains

               Food grains, comprising paddy, pulses, and grains, constitute a
significant category in agriculture. The total cultivated area for food grains
during 2023-24 is 182943.46 Ha. In comparison to the previous year 2022-23, the
area dedicated to food grains has witnessed a decrease of 5.46% during 2023-24.

Paddy

               Paddy cultivated in three seasons in all districts of Kerala except
Wayanad district. In Wayanad there is no autumn paddy cultivation. Area of
paddy is collected in three seasons and its area is estimated in panchayath level
also.
               In the year 1961-’62, the total paddy cultivation area was 7.53 lakh Ha,
and by 1975-’76, it had increased to 8.76 lakh Ha. However, a consistent decline
in paddy cultivation was noted thereafter, reaching 2.29 lakh Ha during the
agricultural year 2007-08. In 2008-09, there was a slight increase, with the area
of paddy cultivation reaching 2.34 lakh Ha.
                 From 2017-18 onwards area of paddy is calculated as the totality of wet
land paddy area and dry land paddy area due to the growing importance of dry
land paddy cultivation.

Season wise - paddy area in Kerala during 2023-24

    Paddy cultivation in Kerala for the year 2023-24 is distributed across
                different seasons, with the majority in the winter season (40%) and the
                least in the autumn season (24.87%).

Autumn Season:

                    Palakkad has the highest paddy cultivation (65.73%) in autumn season
followed by Alappuzha (14.43%), Kottayam (4.47%), and Kannur (4.45%)
districts.

Winter Season:

                    Palakkad has the highest paddy cultivation (40.24%) in winter season
followed by Thrissur (15.53%), Wayanad (9.39%), and Malappuram (8.71%)
districts.

Summer Season:

                    Alappuzha district has the highest paddy cultivation (42.88%) in summer
season followed by Kottayam (17.73%) and Thrissur (17.33%).

(Note: The rankings are based on the district-wise paddy cultivation area in each
respective season.)

                                                     Pulses
      Pulses are cultivated in autumn, winter and summer seasons. The area
under the cultivation of pulses shows a decreasing trend in the state.
       The total area of pulses including tur during 2023-24 is 1589.42 Ha where
            as it was 1547.03 Ha during 2022-23.
       Major cultivation of pulses is in Kannur district in 2023-24 and it was
            618.61 Ha which is 38.92% of the state total. Wayanad and Palakkad
            stands in second and third positions with 16.3% and 10.43% respectively.
       On analyzing the area of last 10 years, cultivation of pulses was the
            maximum during agricultural year 2015-16 with an area of 3764 Ha.
       Major Pulses cultivated are Red gram, Urad, Mung etc.
                                            Sugar Crops
       Two important sugar crops cultivated in our state are sugarcane and
palmyrah. The total area of sugar crops during the period 2023-24 is 2503.67 Ha.
It is decreased by 128.98 Ha compared to 2022-23.

Sugarcane
The total area under cultivation of sugarcane during 2023-24 is 653.28 Ha.
      Idukki district stands first place with 562 Ha area under sugarcane

       20    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                                 Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala


cultivation followed by Alappuzha district with an area of 38.34 Ha during
2023-24. Kottayam and Pathanamthitta districts stands third & fourth positions
with area 25.99 Ha and 18.79 Ha respectievly.
   On analyzing the area of last 10 years, in 2014-15 sugar cane cultivated in
1517.06 Ha area and continuously decreasing in each year.




Palmyrah

         Palmyrah is cultivated in all districts and the contribution of this crop to
total area of sugar crops (sugarcane and palmyrah) is 73.91%. The cultivated
area ranges from 0.29 Ha to 763.05 Ha among the districts, with Palakkad
having the highest and Kannur the lowest. Malappuram, with a Palmyrah
cultivation area of 278.27 Ha units, is the second position, followed by Kottayam
with 201.7 units. The district of Palakkad leads significantly in Palmyrah
cultivation compared to Malappuram and Kottayam.

   The area under cultivation of palmyrah during 2023-24 is increased to
     1850.39 Ha from1702.08 Ha in the previous year.

                                         Spices &Condiments
     The important spices and condiments crops being cultivated in our state are
pepper, ginger, turmeric, cardamom, arecanut, tamarind, cloves, nutmeg,
cinnamon etc. The total area of cultivation of spices & condiments for the
agricultural year 2023-24 is 248941.7 Ha.
     Throughout the years, Idukki district has consistently made a major
contribution to the cultivation of spices & condiments, accounting for 30.56%
during the year 2023-24. Among the specific crops, arecanut holds a substantial

                                             Tubers

    Tubers represented 1.31% area of food crops during the year 2023-24.
Elephant footyam, colocasia, yam, sweet potato, koorka, nanakizhangu,
arrowroot etc include in the category of tubers.
 The total area of tubers during 2023-24 is 11726.04 Ha, where as it was
    12535 Ha during the last year 2022-23.
 Major cultivation of tubers is in Pathanamthitta district and the contribution to
    total area of tubers is 18.70% during 2023-24.
 Kollam (13.84%) and Palakkad (13.71%) districts are in second & third positions
    under the cultivation of tubers in the state during 2022-23.
 Colocasia has first position in area under the cultivation of tubers and the
    percentage of colocasia to the total area of tubers is 40.10%.
   1) Colocasia
               Area during 2023-24 is 4702.64 Ha. Pathanamthitta district stands
          in first position with an area of 967.05 Ha (20.57%). Total area
          decreased by 9.31% with respect to the year 2022-23.

   2) Elephant foot yam
               Area during 2023-24 is 4001.51 Ha. Pathanamthitta district stands
          in first position with an area of 786.15 Ha (19.65%). Total area
          decreased by 10.80% from the year 2022-23.
   3) Yam
               Area during 2023-24 is 1140.67 Ha which is decreased by 7.71%
          than the previous year. Pathanamthitta district stands in first position
          with an area of 371.75 Ha and is least in Thrissur district and the
          contribution to total area during 2022-23 is only 0.42% (4.78 Ha) .
   4) Sweet Potato
               Area during 2023-24 is 150.39 Ha. Kasargod district stands in first
          with an area of 36.14 Ha (24.03%) and Malappuram district stands in
          second position with an area of 33.79 Ha (22.47%). There is a slight
          increase of 0.26% in the cultivation of sweet potato this year as against
          2022-23.

    5) Koorka
               Area during 2023-24 is 1133.08 Ha. Total area increased by 33.65%
           with respect to the year 2022-23. Palakkad district stands in first
           position with an area of 864.92 Ha (76.34%) and is least in

                                               Amaranthus
     Amaranthus is the third major vegetable by cultivation area and it is 1952.88.
In 2022-23 the area was 1929.86. Thiruvananthapuram District leads in cultivation
with 273.70 Ha and Alappuzha is second with area 269.97. Wayand District has the
least cultivation area of 56.51.

                                                Oil Seeds
     Important oil seeds being cultivated in our state are coconut, groundnut,
sesamum etc. Coconut represents 99.62% in the category of oil seeds. The total
area under the cultivation of oil seeds during the agricultural year 2023-24 is
768762.59 Ha. On comparing with 2022-23, a slight increase of 0.70% can be
seen in this category during the year 2023-24. A brief analysis of important oil
seeds is given below.

         Coconut
    Considering the area under cultivation of crops, coconut occupies first place
among them. Area under coconut cultivation was 6.93 lakhs Ha during 1975-76,
7.05 lakh Ha during 1985-86 and 9.14 lakh Ha during 1995-96. The area under
coconut cultivation reached highest during 2000-01 i.e., 9.26 lakhs Ha.
Thereafter, a decreasing tendency is seen in the area under the cultivation of
coconut in Kerala.

                    CROP AREA UTILIZATION OVER TIME




                         Fibre, Drugs and Narcotics

        Crops like cotton, betel leaves, tobacco, and lemongrass are included
in this category. In the agricultural year 2023-24, the total cultivation area of
fiber, drugs, and narcotics amounted to 280.73 Ha, marking a decrease from
the 343.98 Ha recorded in 2022-23. Betel leaves held the leading position in
cultivation area within this category, covering 220.75 Ha in 2023-24, followed
by lemongrass with 49.68 Ha. However, the area of betel leaves was 207.09
Ha in 2022-23, and for lemongrass, it was 124.69 Ha in 2022-23.

    Cotton
        The cultivated area in 2023-24 amounts to 6.5 Ha, exclusively in
        Palakkad district. There has been 25% increase in cotton cultivation
        this year as compared to the preceding year, 2022-23.

   Betel leaves
        In 2023-24, the total cultivated area for betel leaves amounted to
        220.75 Ha, with Malappuram leading at 109.14 Ha. There has been an
        increase of 6.59% in the cultivation area of betel leaves this year
        compared to the previous year, 2022-23.


 37   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                                     Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




        Lemongrass
                   In 2023-24, the total area of lemongrass cultivation amounted to
               49.68 Ha, with Idukki claiming the top position with 45.55 Ha. There
               has been a 60.16% reduction in the cultivation area of lemongrass
               compared to the previous year, 2022-23.

        Tobacco
               In 2023-24 3.8 Ha of tobacco were cultivated in Kerala, specifically in
               Kasargod district. There has been a decrease in the tobacco cultivation
               area compared to the preceding year, 2022-23 which was 7 Ha.


                                         Plantation Crops

   In our state, significant plantation crops encompass tea, coffee, rubber, and
cocoa.
           The collective area dedicated to plantation crops in 2023-24 stood at
            684403.10 Ha, slightly lower than the 684294.61 Ha recorded in 2022-23,
            marking a decrease of 0.02%.
           Kottayam district holds a prominent position in plantation crop
            cultivation, contributing 16.85% to the total area dedicated to these crops.
           Rubber dominates the cultivation of plantation crops, claiming the top
            position with a representation of 80.51% in the total cultivated area.

                                                 Rubber
   In 2023-24, the area of rubber cultivation amounted to 551030 Ha.

           In the rubber cultivation for the year 2023-24, Kottayam claimed the top
            spot, cultivating 114250 Ha of rubber, which represents 20.73% of the
            total rubber cultivation area.
           Ernakulam secured the second position, contributing 10.91% of the total
            rubber cultivation area. Pathanamthitta followed closely behind, claiming
            the third position with 9.23% of the total rubber cultivation area.

                                          CHAPTER 3

                                 CROP PRODUCTION
                                  STATISTICS 2023-24
                                     The growth of an agricultural economy is
                    depending on mainly on three factors viz, increasing crop
                    productivity, employment generation and raising farmer’s
                    income. Crop production and productivity the key components of
                    food security as it is essential to feed a growing population.
                    According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the
                    United Nations, farmers globally must increase the agriculture
                    crop production by 70 percent before the year 2050 in order to
                    meet the demands. But the trend in the agricultural data for
                    past years shows that it would not be happen. Since agriculture
                    sector is facing severe land fragmentation and changes in soil
                    structure and texture due to unscientific water resource
                    management and indiscriminate use of fertilisers. Moreover,
                    agriculture yields are increasingly being affected by climate
                    change.
                                  To meet the demand of the population,
                    agricultural production through efficient resource management
                    and modern agricultural practices should be increased. This
                    involves the use of high yield or improved crop varieties, for
                    precise application of agricultural inputs based on soil, weather
                    and crop requirement. Such practices maximise productivity,
                    quality and profitability in a sustainable manner. Assessment
                    of current production data is key to mould strategies to achieve
                    this goal. This chapter is intended to make insights of the same
                    providing detailed information on production and productivity
                    of major and minor crops in the state.




191   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                              Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




GENERAL CROP ESTIMATION SURVEY

         The General Crop Estimation Survey (GCES) under the EARAS scheme,
conducted parallel to the Land Utilization Survey, collects annual data on crop
production and productivity of major and minor crops in Kerala for each
agricultural year. Crop yield estimates are derived from scientifically designed
Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) conducted at the field level. The GCES covers
11 major crops and 6 minor crops annually as follows.

Major Crops - Paddy, Tapioca, Coconut, Arecanut, Cashew, Pepper,

                    Cocoa, Banana, Plantain, Sesamum, Jack.

Minor crops - Ginger, Turmeric, Nutmeg, Betel leaves, Pineapple, Sugarcane.

         For the following crops production and productivity are estimated by
conducting crop cutting experiments in irregular years. Using this productivity
the projected estimates are used for subsequent years. For the 2023-24
agricultural year, the selected minor crops are Papaya and Drumstick. The
estimates are given in Table 4.



         Tamarind, Cloves, Mango, Sweet potato, Bitter guard, Green chillies,
         Cowpea, Cucumber, Snake gourd, Brinjal, Elephant foot yam, Lady's
         finger, Colocasia, Papaya, Drumstick


Besides, for the following crops the advance estimates are given in Table 4.


         Cholam/Jower, Ragi/Finger millet (koovaraku), Maize, Small millet
         (Thina/Chama), Tur/Red gram, Gram, Other pulses, Garlic, Bajra,
         Mustard, Ground nut, Cotton, Tobacco, Sun flower

         Paddy, the primary crop extensively cultivated across all districts of the
state, follows a distinct three-season pattern: Autumn (July-October), Winter
(November-February), and Summer (March-June). In 2023-24 agricultural year,
the highest rice production has occurred during the winter season, contributing
2,12,261.967 tonnes, which is accounted for 39.82% of the state's total rice
production. This is followed by the summer season, producing 2,04,795.773
tonnes (38.40%), while the autumn season yields 1,16,269.383 tonnes (21.80%).




   194    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                                                                                    Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




         Palakkad district consistently retains its position as the highest rice
producer, with a production of 1,82,380.716 tonnes, while Idukki has recorded
the lowest at 819.076 tonnes. Alappuzha, Thrissur, and Kottayam ranks second,
third, and fourth, respectively. Together, these four districts contribute 82.53% of
Kerala’s total rice production.
         Analysing rice production by district and season, Palakkad remains the
top producer during the autumn and winter seasons, whereas Alappuzha has
recorded the highest production during the summer season in the 2023-24
agricultural year.

                               Palakkad is the largest producer of bananas in Kerala, accounting for

producing districts in Kerala during the 2023-24 agricultural year.

                                                 CHAPTER 4

                                      TREND ANALYSIS
                                                This chapter provides an analysis of the
                               area, production and productivity of six major crops –
                               paddy (season – wise), coconut, arecanut, pepper,
                               banana and tapioca – over the period from 2014-15 to
                               2023-24. These crops are vital to agricultural
                               economies, particularly in regions like Kerala, where
                               they contribute significantly to livelihoods and food
                               security. The report begins by examining variations in
                               net    cropped     area    and     land   diverted     to   non-
                               agricultural       use,    highlighting     shifts    in    land
                               utilization patterns over the decade. This analysis
                               aims       to   inform    policymakers,     researchers      and
                               stakeholders       about     the     evolving      agricultural
                               landscape and its implications for sustainability and
                               economic development.




291   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                             Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




TREND ANALYSIS ON NET AREA SOWN & LAND PUT TO
NON-AGRICULTURAL USE FROM 2014-15 TO 2023-24

        The land utilization trends in Kerala from 2014-15 to 2023-24 reveal
notable changes. Non-agricultural land use increased significantly from
419,128.00 hectares in 2014-15 to 502,608.91 hectares in 2023-24, marking an
overall rise of 19.92%. This trend has remained consistently upward, with no
years showing a decline. In contrast, the net area sown has decreased from
2,042,881.00 hectares in 2014-15 to 1,972,769.72 hectares in 2023-24, showing
an overall decline of 3.43%. While this metric has shown some fluctuations, the
general trend is downward. These opposing patterns suggest a conversion of
agricultural land for non-agricultural purposes. Moreover, the rate at which
non-agricultural land is expanding surpasses the decline in net sown area,
indicating that additional land sources are also being converted.




  292    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                              Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




TREND ANALYSIS ON AREA, PRODUCTION AND YIELD
FOR MAJOR CROPS FROM 2014-15 TO 2023-24

             The crop-wise trend analysis based on the data from the
 agricultural year 2014-15 to 2023-24 focusing on Area, Production, and Yield
 for the crops Paddy, Coconut, Arecanut, Pepper, Banana, and Tapioca are
 summarised below.


                                           PADDY
Autumn Paddy
         Analysing the data on autumn paddy area decreased from 63,981 ha in
 2014-15 to 44,844 ha in 2023-24. There is a 30% decline in area. Production
 dropped from 161,477 tons to 116,269 tons (28% decline), with a low of
 101,943 tons in 2018-19 and a peak of 167,181 tons in 2016-17. Yield
 fluctuated between 1,679 kg/ha in 2018-19 and 2,954 kg/ha in 2016-17,
 ending at 2,593 kg/ha in 2023-24. There has been 3% increase from 2014-15
 to 2023-24. On observing the trend consistent reduction in area and
 production, with yield showing variability but a slight overall improvement.




 293   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                            Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




Winter Paddy
       Analysing the data on winter paddy over 10 years, area decreased from
88,990 ha in 2014-15 to 72,107 ha in 2023-24 which shows a 19% decline, with
a low of 71,430 ha in 2022-23. Production fell from 254,450 tons to 212,262
tons (17% decline), peaking at 281,035 tons in 2020-21. Yield increased from
2,859 kg/ha to 2,944 kg/ha (3% rise), peaking at 3,175 kg/ha in 2020-21. Trend
shows a declining in area and production, with modest yield gains.




Summer Paddy


              The data on Summer Paddy in Kerala as presented reveals a
distinctive trend. Area increased from 45,188 ha (2014-15) to 63,327 ha (2023-
24). There is a 40% increase, peaking at 69,822 ha in 2022-23. Production rise
from 146165 tons to 204796 tons peaking at 233880 tons in 2022-23. There has
been 40% increase in production of Summer Paddy from 2014-15 to 2023-24.
The highest production is in 2022-23 at 233880, indicating favourable weather
conditions during that period. On analysing the yield data negligible changes
can be seen. Yield remained relatively stable moving from 3235 kg/ha to 3234
kg/ha with a peak of 4028 kg/ha in 2018-19. Trend shows a significant growth
in area and production with yield stable.



 294   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                              Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




Total Paddy
         Analysing the data on paddy cultivated area in Kerala from 2014-15 to
2023-24 reveals several fluctuations. Initially, from 2014-15 to 2016-17, there
was a gradual decline in paddy cultivated area, with a significant decrease from
1,98,159 hectares in 2014-15 to 1,71,398 hectares in 2016-17. This decline may
be attributed to various factors such as changes in climate. However, from 2016-
17 onwards, there seems to be a stabilization or slight increase in the cultivation
area upto 2020-21. A similar pattern to the cultivation area can be observed in
paddy production also, except for a deviation between 2018-19 and 2019-20.




   295    | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                                  Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala



         During 2016-17 Kerala witnessed a sudden decline in area, production and
productivity of paddy. When considering the season wise data it was observed
that this sudden decline was observed during winter 2016-17. The climatic
conditions during this period indicated that it was seriously affeced the paddy
area production, and productivity since kerala faced a large deficit in north east
monsoon, especially in December 2016.
         The agricultural year 2018-19, kerala faced extremely heavy rainfall and
flood and it severely affected paddy area, production and productivity. The data
shows that during autumn 2018 -19, paddy production declined to 101943 tonnes
from 148913 tonnes in previous year, with critical loss in productivity also. How
ever, it was not much affected total paddy production and productivity since it
regained it's stability during winter and summer 2018 -19 agricultural year.
         From 2020-21 onwards, data indicates that paddy area, production, and
productivity have shown a declining trend during the COVID-19 and post-
COVID periods. Farmers faced significant challenges in market access and
economic losses, particularly during the lockdown. However, the public
procurement system functioned effectively, helping to prevent a major economic
crisis during that time. Efficient management of paddy procurement, along with
other precautionary measures, played a key role in avoiding a more drastic
decline.
                                               COCONUT

                 The data on Coconut cultivation reveals a minor decline in area,
  production, and yield over the years. Specifically, the area dedicated to
  coconut farming has slightly decreased from 793,856 hectares in 2014-15 to
  765,842 hectares in 2023-24, representing a decline of approximately 4%.
  Production has fallen from 5,947 million nuts to 5,523 million nuts, marking a
  decline of around 7%, with a notable low of 4,788 million nuts recorded in
  2020-21. Similarly, the yield has decreased from 7,491 nuts per hectare to
  7,211 nuts per hectare, reflecting a 4% decline, with the lowest yield of 6,228
  nuts per hectare also occurring in 2020-21. Overall, these trends indicate a
  minor reduction in both area and production, alongside a slight downward
  trend in yield, suggesting the need for attention to the factors influencing
  coconut cultivation.


   296     | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                           Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




                                      ARECANUT


      The data on Arecanut cultivation indicates a stable area with a slight
decline, alongside a notable reduction in both production and yield.
Specifically, the area dedicated to arecanut farming has decreased marginally
from 96,686 hectares in 2014-15 to 96,113 hectares in 2023-24, reflecting a
decline of approximately 1%, albeit with some fluctuations. In terms of
production, there has been a significant drop from 125,926 tons to 103,985
tons, representing a decline of around 17%, with production peaking at
132,453 tons in 2015-16. Similarly, the yield has decreased from 1,302 kg/ha to
1,082 kg/ha, also reflecting a 17% decline, with the highest yield recorded at
1,336 kg/ha in 2015-16. Overall, these trends highlight a stable area but a
concerning reduction in production and yield, suggesting the need for further
investigation into the factors affecting arecanut cultivation.




297   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                              Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




                                          PEPPER
      The Pepper cultivation indicates a concerning trend characterized by a
decline in area, production, and yield over the years. Specifically, the area
dedicated to pepper farming has decreased from 85,431 hectares in 2014-15 to
72,669 hectares in 2023-24, representing a reduction of approximately 15%.
Production has similarly declined from 40,690 metric tons to 30,798 metric
tons, marking a decline of around 24%, despite peaking at 42,132 metric tons
in 2015-16. Yield has also dropped from 476 kg/ha to 424 kg/ha, reflecting an
11% decline, with a peak yield of 490 kg/ha in 2015-16. Overall, these trends
highlight a significant reduction in both the area and production of pepper,
alongside a decline in yield following an initial peak, suggesting the need for
further investigation into the factors affecting pepper cultivation.




298   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                             Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




                                          BANANA

        The data on Banana cultivation reveals a significant reduction in area,
a moderate decline in production, and a notable improvement in yield.
Specifically, the area dedicated to banana farming has decreased from 61,936
hectares in 2014-15 to 47,542 hectares in 2023-24, representing a decline of
approximately 23%. In terms of production, there has been a drop from
545,431 tons to 477,521 tons, marking a decline of around 12%, despite
peaking at 565,829 tons in 2017-18. Interestingly, the yield has increased from
8,806 kg/ha to 10,044kg/ha, reflecting a rise of approximately 14%, with this
peak yield occurring in 2023-24. Overall, these trends indicate a concerning
reduction in the area allocated for banana cultivation and a decline in
production, while the significant improvement in yield suggests advancements
in agricultural practices or conditions that may warrant further exploration.




299   | Agricultural Statistics 2023-24
                                              Department of Economics and Statistics, Kerala




                                          TAPIOCA
      The data on Tapioca cultivation indicates a notable reduction in area, a
moderate decline in production, and a consistent improvement in yield.
Specifically, the area dedicated to tapioca farming has declined from 75,493
hectares in 2014-15 to 55,869 hectares in 2023-24, representing a significant
reduction of approximately 26%. Production has decreased from 2,943,919
tons to 2,365,765 tons, marking a decline of around 20%, despite peaking at
3,027,750 tons in 2020-21. Interestingly, the yield has increased from 38,996
kg/ha to 42,345 kg/ha, reflecting a rise of approximately 9%, with the highest
yield recorded at 47,127 kg/ha in 2020-21. ie. during the Covid-19 period
(2020-21), tapioca farming performed very well. Productivity and production
improved significantly, possibly because farmers might have focussed more on
food crops, better management practices or favourable weather conditions.
Overall, these trends highlight a concerning reduction in the area allocated for
tapioca cultivation and a decline in production, while the consistent
improvement in yield suggests advancements in agricultural practices or
conditions that may warrant further investigation.
